title: A treatment can do better in every group and still look worse overall
body: In a 1986 study of kidney stone treatments, treatment A (open surgery) beat treatment B (closed procedures) for small stones, 93% to 87%, and for large stones, 73% to 69%. Yet with all patients pooled, B looked better: 83% to 78%. Doctors tended to give A to large stones, the hard cases that fail more often, and B to small ones, so A's total was dragged down by its difficult cases. This is **Simpson's paradox**: a trend inside every group can vanish or reverse when the groups are combined, so ask what drives the numbers before concluding anything about cause and effect.

slides.question: Treatment A cured 93% of small kidney stones and 73% of large ones. What was its success rate over all its patients?
slides.explanation: 78%, or 273 of 350 patients. Not halfway between: 263 of A's 350 patients had large stones, so its overall rate sits close to the 73%.

slides.alt: Infographic animation: one dot per patient for two kidney stone treatments. Treatment A wins for small stones, 93% to 87%, and for large stones, 73% to 69%, but when the groups are pooled B wins, 83% to 78%. Balance beams show why: A treated mostly large stones.

slides.prompt: A wins with small stones and with large ones, yet loses overall. Change how many hard cases each treatment gets until A wins overall too.
slides.takeaway: With the same mix of cases, A wins overall as well. The reversal came from A being given the hard cases, not from A being worse.

slides.heading: Kidney stone success rates: A wins both rounds, B wins overall
slides.note: From a 1986 study comparing two treatments for kidney stones, 350 patients each.

slides.heading: The hidden factor
slides.text: Stone size mattered more than the treatment: large stones failed more often whichever treatment was used. And 263 of A's 350 patients had large stones, against 80 of B's. A factor like this, which shapes both who gets a treatment and how it turns out, is called a confounder.

slides.heading: Berkeley, 1973
slides.text: That autumn, 44% of men who applied to Berkeley's graduate school were admitted, against 35% of women. But women had applied more often to competitive departments with low admission rates. Corrected for department, the pooled data showed a "small but statistically significant bias in favor of women".

slides.question: In the kidney stone study, why did treatment A look worse overall?
options: The percentages were added up wrongly
B’s patients were younger and fitter
A was mostly used on the harder cases
A’s small-stone results were left out
slides.explanation: Treatment A was mostly given for large stones, the harder cases that fail more often, while B mostly got easy small stones. Stone size, the hidden factor, skewed the totals.
